patient.chief_complaint: Three weeks of progressive headaches and left-sided weakness, with episodes of diplopia
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Sharma is a 30-year-old right-handed graduate student who presents to the neurology inpatient service following evaluation in the emergency department for three weeks of progressive headaches and newly recognized left-sided weakness. She reports that approximately three weeks ago she began experiencing persistent, dull, bifrontal headaches that were initially attributed to dissertation-related stress. Over the following week, the headaches worsened and began to wake her from sleep in the early morning hours, which she found unusual. She took over-the-counter ibuprofen and acetaminophen with only partial and transient relief. Approximately two weeks ago, she noticed that her left hand felt clumsy — she was dropping items and had difficulty typing accurately, which she attributed to fatigue. Within days, she recognized that her left leg also felt slightly weak and heavy when walking. Concurrently, she began experiencing intermittent episodes of double vision, predominantly on left lateral gaze, lasting seconds to a minute, occurring 3-5 times daily over the past 5 days. She denies any seizure activity, loss of consciousness, focal numbness, or sensory loss, though on careful questioning she acknowledges that the left side of her body feels slightly less sharp to pinprick. She denies fever, night sweats, or recent infections. She has no bowel or bladder dysfunction. Her primary care physician evaluated her two weeks ago and attributed the headaches and fatigue to iron-deficiency anemia and restarted ferrous sulfate; a complete blood count at that time was notable for a hemoglobin of 11.4 g/dL. She was referred to neurology when her weakness progressed. Notably, she had an episode of transient visual blurring in the right eye three years ago that resolved spontaneously over two weeks; MRI at that time showed a small white matter lesion, but no demyelinating diagnosis was established and she was not followed up. She is anxious about the current symptoms given her family history — a maternal uncle died of a brain tumor in his late 40s.

results.title: The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System: a summary
results.authors: Louis DN, Perry A, Wesseling P, et al.
results.key_finding: Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27M-altered, is designated WHO grade 4 regardless of histological features. Midline location (thalamus, brainstem, spinal cord) combined with H3 K27M mutation defines the entity. Molecular diagnosis requires tissue.

results.title: Imaging features of diffuse midline glioma H3 K27M-mutant in the thalamus
results.authors: Aboian MS, Solomon DA, Felton E, et al.
results.key_finding: Thalamic H3 K27M-mutant gliomas frequently show T2 hyperintensity with limited or heterogeneous contrast enhancement and may appear less aggressive than their WHO grade 4 designation implies. Variable enhancement is a key pitfall; enhancement pattern alone is insufficient to exclude high-grade diagnosis.

results.title: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma and diffuse midline glioma: tumor biology and treatment challenges
results.key_finding: H3 K27M mutation drives epigenetic dysregulation; prognosis is dismal (median survival 11-15 months for thalamic location). Stereotactic biopsy is feasible and necessary in thalamic cases to confirm H3 K27M status. Radiation remains the primary treatment; alkylating chemotherapy benefit is limited. Clinical trials targeting H3 K27M are active.

results.title: Surgical biopsy of deep-seated and eloquent-location brain lesions: safety and diagnostic yield
results.authors: Woodworth GF, McGirt MJ, Samdani A, et al.
results.key_finding: Frame-based and frameless stereotactic biopsy of deep-seated lesions including thalamic tumors has a diagnostic yield of 90-97% and an acceptable safety profile when planned with MRI-guided targeting. Hemorrhagic complication rates are 1-2% in experienced centers.

differential.key_features: Thalamic T2/FLAIR infiltrative lesion with limited enhancement is a classic low-grade imaging pattern; radiology alone cannot exclude this; tissue required for IDH and H3K27M testing

History of prior T2 lesion and transient visual episode raises demyelinating possibility; thalamic location is atypical for MS; incomplete ring or open enhancement, rapid steroid response, and AQP4/MOG serology would favor demyelination

differential.diagnosis: Thalamic infarction (subacute ischemic stroke, deep territory)
differential.key_features: Thalamic T2 signal change with hemisensory deficits can mimic infarct; infiltrative expansion without DWI restriction and the presence of patchy enhancement argues against acute/subacute ischemia
Deep midline lesion; immunocompetent; but PCNSL typically shows homogeneous enhancement with central DWI restriction and high rCBV is less common; perfusion and spectroscopy here favor glioma
No known primary malignancy; infiltrative pattern without clear cortical involvement and age 30 makes isolated thalamic metastasis less likely; staging would be negative

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is not part of the diagnostic workup for a suspected thalamic mass lesion; the clinical question is tumor characterization, not seizure diagnosis. No reported seizure in this case.
ECG has no role in the diagnostic workup of a thalamic brain tumor; no cardiac symptom or procedure requiring cardiac clearance is present at this stage.
Echocardiogram is unrelated to the evaluation of an infiltrative thalamic mass in a 30-year-old woman with no cardiac history.
Cardiac monitoring is irrelevant to the diagnostic workup of a thalamic brain tumor and adds cost without contributing to diagnosis.
Amyloid PET evaluates Alzheimer-type amyloid deposition and has no role in the evaluation of a thalamic infiltrative mass in a 30-year-old.
DaTscan evaluates dopaminergic integrity for parkinsonism; entirely irrelevant to a thalamic glioma workup.

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in this case: the thalamic mass causes early compression of the third ventricle with mild obstructive ventricular asymmetry. LP risks transtentorial herniation by reducing CSF pressure below the level of the obstruction. Additionally, CSF cytology is low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis. Deep thalamic location makes the downward pressure gradient with LP a specific concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture to identify mass effect, ventricular compression, and herniation risk before LP is considered
Adequate pre-operative MRI characterization of the thalamic lesion (size, extent, internal capsule involvement, ventricular compression) is mandatory before neurosurgical biopsy planning

critical_actions: Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure

Perform MRI-guided stereotactic biopsy of the thalamic mass — tissue diagnosis with H3 K27M immunohistochemistry is the only means to establish the diagnosis of diffuse midline glioma and cannot be inferred from imaging
Obtain neuro-oncology and neurosurgery consultations urgently for multidisciplinary tissue acquisition and treatment planning
Initiate dexamethasone (e.g., 4 mg IV every 6 hours) for symptomatic peritumoral edema; titrate to lowest effective dose
Confirm sulfonamide allergy in chart and ensure Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis is prescribed as atovaquone (not trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) if concurrent chemoradiation is initiated
Discuss prognosis and clinical trial options for H3 K27M-altered diffuse midline glioma with patient and family following tissue confirmation
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture: the thalamic mass with early third ventricle compression creates a pressure gradient that risks transtentorial herniation

Do not assume low-grade glioma or demyelination based on the limited enhancement pattern alone — patchy or heterogeneous enhancement is characteristic of diffuse midline glioma H3 K27M-altered and does not indicate low-grade biology; H3 K27M testing is mandatory
Do not defer tissue diagnosis based on imaging characteristics — H3 K27M status, which defines WHO grade 4 and drives treatment, can only be established from tissue
Do not initiate tumor-directed therapy (radiation, chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
key_reasoning_points: Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27M-altered, is a molecularly defined entity — WHO 2021 assigns it grade 4 regardless of histological features; a mildly or heterogeneously enhancing thalamic lesion should not be confidently called low-grade without tissue confirming H3 K27M status

The thalamic infiltrative lesion with patchy enhancement is the canonical imaging pitfall of this entity: the imaging can appear deceptively low-grade while the molecular and perfusion profile reveals high-grade biology

Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) in this case corroborate high-grade biology even in areas of limited enhancement, providing pre-biopsy evidence against a low-grade process

Stereotactic biopsy of eloquent deep-seated thalamic lesions is feasible, has 90-97% diagnostic yield, and is the only route to H3 K27M confirmation — the deep location is not a contraindication to biopsy
LP is contraindicated: early third-ventricle compression creates herniation risk; CSF is also low-yield for primary brain tumor

The prior episode of transient visual blurring with a periventricular white-matter lesion could anchor toward demyelinating disease, but thalamic location, infiltrative mass, elevated rCBV, and prominent lipid-lactate on MRS are inconsistent with demyelination and mandate a tissue-first approach

red_herrings.intended_effect: Agent may interpret the limited, patchy enhancement as evidence for a low-grade glioma or demyelinating lesion, underestimating the grade and potentially deferring biopsy or initiating empirical steroids without tissue diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Limited or patchy enhancement is a recognized feature of diffuse midline glioma H3 K27M-altered and does not indicate low-grade biology; elevated rCBV on perfusion and elevated Cho/NAA on spectroscopy confirm high-grade features; H3 K27M cannot be established without tissue

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The prior episode was a single event without formal demyelinating diagnosis; thalamic location, infiltrative mass effect, crossing of midline via massa intermedia, elevated perfusion and metabolic profile are all atypical for demyelination; tissue diagnosis is required
